To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we can compress a CNN by replacing its standard convolutions with depthwise separable convolutions, while retaining its classification accuracy.

depthwise separable convolutions are a special case of standard convolutions and that the number of depthwise separable layers should be chosen carefully to match the accuracy of standard convolutions.

depthwise separable convolutions can be used to approximate a standard convolution, and that the accuracy of the approximation is related to the number of depthwise separable layers and to the number of filters in each of these layers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How can we design a depthwise separable CNN with a similar accuracy to a standard CNN?
the following questions: How can we understand depthwise separable convolutions? How can we efficiently train them? How can we compress CNNs based on depthwise convolutions?
the following questions: (i) Can we theoretically analyze the relations between the standard convolution and its depthwise separable counterpart?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

1) depthwise separable CNNs are not as powerful as standard convolutional CNNs; 2) depthwise separability does not always help compressing CNNs; and 3) depthwise separably compressed CNNs are less accurate than standard CNNs.
the depthwise separable convolutions are a lossy compression scheme that is not able to retain the accuracy of the standard convolution.

depthwise separable convolutions can be used to replace the standard convolution in CNNs, and they can be applied in a variety of ways to achieve a better accuracy-compactness trade-off than the standard convolution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a new convolution operator, called Fast and Lightweight ConvNet (FALCON), which is based on the depthwise separable structure and is more efficient and effective than previous works.
we provide a theoretical foundation for depthwise separable convolutions, and propose FALCON, a fast and lightweight convolution that can be used to replace standard convolution in CNNs.
we provide a precise understanding of depthwise separable convolutions, and show how to leverage this understanding to compress CNNs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
depthwise separable convolutions are not only efficient but also accurate, and we show that they have a strong theoretical foundation.
we can efficiently compress CNN while retaining their accuracy using depthwise separable convolutions.
depthwise separable and standard convolution are related through the notion of the “convolution kernel”, a generalization of the convolution filter.
